title: Research the Organisation, Not Only the User
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Research the Organisation, Not Only the User.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Products are made inside organisations. Stakeholder and organisational research examines goals, constraints, vocabulary, incentives, decision rights, workflows, policies, technical dependencies, and measures. It does not replace user research; it explains what the organisation can change and where a user problem is being produced.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interview people across roles, inspect artifacts and handoffs, and map where a decision becomes a rule, a system behaviour, or a support burden. Treat internal claims as evidence with a perspective, not as neutral truth. A leader’s target, an engineer’s constraint, and a support agent’s recurring issue can all be valid while pointing to different intervention points.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Study how the service produces behaviour
turns.text: What changes when we look at study how the service produces behaviour?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interview and observe frontline staff, operations, policy, support, sales, data, engineering, risk, and leadership where relevant. Review process, incentives, targets, decision rights, tools, handoffs, capacity, and workarounds. Compare the official service with what people do to keep it working.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Organisational constraints are not automatically fixed facts. Ask which are legal, technical, strategic, historical, or incentive-created; who owns them; and what evidence could change them. A policy described as mandatory may be local interpretation. A manual workaround may contain valuable expertise or conceal unsafe dependence.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Map customer and organisational evidence together. Trace a visible friction backward to queue, data, authority, or metric. Protect staff confidentiality and avoid using research as performance surveillance.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Translate findings into system choices and accountable owners. User research that repeatedly recommends clearer copy while internal rules create the confusion is scoped too narrowly.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Study the system that produces the experience
turns.text: What changes when we look at study the system that produces the experience?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The team compares the official process with observed work. Workarounds are neither celebrated nor removed automatically: they may protect patients from a policy or tooling failure. Findings identify where a product change is possible, where operational change is required, and where leadership must resolve a constraint.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at failure modes in practice?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Constraint theatre: historical choices are described as immutable law. Leadership truth: senior stakeholder accounts are treated as neutral system facts. Staff surveillance: observation exposes individuals instead of diagnosing work conditions. Interface collapse: every organisational finding becomes a screen or copy request.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ownerless recommendation: the intervention sits outside the authority of anyone in the decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Trace the production of one customer-visible state
turns.text: What changes when we look at trace the production of one customer-visible state?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The organisational study uses semi-structured interviews, job shadowing, artefact review, decision-right mapping, and service data. Role accounts are compared because each person sees a different slice. A clinic manager may describe official weekly release, while coordinators reserve capacity informally for complex cases and engineers see delayed supplier updates.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Contradiction is mapped to the workflow rather than resolved by seniority.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The output is a constraint-and-change map. It distinguishes law, clinical rule, contract, policy, technical limitation, capacity, historical habit, and incentive. For each, the team records who can change it and what evidence is required. This turns “the business will not allow it” into a set of accountable decisions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: refund delay?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customers may understand a refund screen perfectly while finance batches approvals, fraud review lacks context, and support cannot see settlement. Organisational research reveals that clearer copy cannot fulfil the promise; the service needs event definitions, authority, and an escalation route.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Organisational research makes power and changeability visible. Distinguish a lawful or safety constraint from a local interpretation, a missing capability, or an incentive leaders could change. Protect staff evidence from becoming performance surveillance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Customers complain that refunds take too long. Interviews reveal frustration, but the cause sits in a finance policy, a handoff between two teams, a legacy data field, and a service metric that rewards fast closure rather than resolution.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose one frustrating customer-facing rule. Trace who created it, who operates it, which system encodes it, what measure reinforces it, and who has authority to change it.
